review:
I'll start off by saying that it is extremely addicting and worth the money.

The game begins by giving you a 30 second tutorial then literally thrusting you into the game, expecting you to use trial and error to succeed. As you play the game you will get more efficient each play through as you learn more about how the game works and what strategies are good in the early mid and late game.

Pros:
+ Sound Track is on Point
+ Visual Style is appealing
+ Proggression is strong
+ Extremely Difficult, forcing you to adapt
+ Money is your health and you can't hold an infinite amount of money

Cons:
- Lack of story
- Horse Stamina (When your kingdom gets massive it's extremely annoying to stop and recover stamina)
- Lack of Late game monsters (There are essentially 3 monster types)

Questionable Design Decisions:
= Extremely Fast Day and NIght Cycles
= Only One Wave of monsters per Night. Becomes kind of exploitable
= Limited to building 4 knights (2 per side) Allowing more knights could have enabled more difficult attacks from the
monsters and more preperations by the player.

= The only way to get new people to your Kingdom is to hire them at camps. The system limits expansion speed but  causes the player to constantly run back and forth accross the map to recruit new people.

OVERVIEW:
Simplistic game that is worth the money. 

One word of advice. Don't stand too close to your catapults.

A lot of people with negative reviews are complaining about bad AI of workers and bad aim of archers. I'm not sure what the devs planned for the game but I see the "bad" AI as intentional. Basically if you give a worker or workers a job they will mindlessly try to complete the job. People complain that this is stupid because workers will go out in the middle of the night to their deaths until the project is complete. I see this as a positive thing. Say you desperately need to repair a torn down wall right as the day turns to night. Would you rather your workers stand in the safety of your kingdom or go and repair the wall as you told them to. If you plan out the jobs you give to your workers you shouldn't have a problem with all your workers going out at night to their doom to chop down a tree.

Wow that was a lot of stuff. But I'm not done yet. 

On to the topic of Archers and their terrible aim.
I think Archers are meant to be inaccurate so that when they hunt during the day they don't bring in so much gold as to break the early game. A lone Archer is not very powerful, but as you recruit more people, the relentless volleys of arrows released by 15+ archers is hard to beat. Sure one archer can miss an enemy 5 times in a row but 10 archers will easily dispatch exponentially more enemies then a small group can. What I'm trying to say is that the game is balanced around recruiting. Expanding and not destroying ecampments so that you can recruit constantly. The more archers you have the more powerful your kingdom is. Rapid and early Recruitment is better than expansion because people are power. There is a good saying in Kingdom. "If your not recruiting your losing"

So, after over 40 hours spent playing the game I felt it's time to finally write a review.

First of all, I really enjoy this game tremendously, but I'd say it's not for everyone. If you read other reviews, you probably have a good idea what the good part of the game is, nice art, awesome soundtrack (first time I ever bought a game OST, and not regretting it one bit). These are the two things I think everyone can agree about.

Then it gets more tricky. The gameplay isn't for everyone. It's literally discover everything for yourself. including how your own guys behave, even how your own horse behaves.
The real problem can come from when you don't figure some things out (like how to keep your horse running or how to make your dudes not suicide themselves constantly) and then give up thinking the devs didn't think of that and write review claiming the game is unfinished or lacking.

On the other hand, simply reading a guide after 5 hours of play, is basically ruining the discovery experience, so in my opinion if you want to enjoy the game try to not look up too many things (or maybe just ask a simple singe question in the forums instead).

Now, that being said, another big deterrent can be the lack of endgame content. (It needs to be said though, that the devs are working on adding more stuff (for free), so that might not be true anyore in a few months.)
For me, it took me over 10 hours to beat the game the first time I think, and after that, there where achievements for doing it quick and for enduring long. The speedrunning aspect I really liked, but the endurance aspect (trying to survive as long as you can) is really lacking atm. Once you're set up there's not much to do for 30-50 days, cause you're defenses are just that good.
So if you really enjoy building up a large empire and surviving a long time, this game is in it's current stage definitely not for you (imo).
Me personally, I really enjoy the speedrunning aspect of the game, so trying over and over to finish the game quicker and quicker is really fun for me and is mostly what kept me going for the last 25 hours or so. (Especially since people keep getting quicker and quicker :D)
It also means that one has to learn more and more details about the game mechanics, which I really like too. I've played over 40 hours and still learn new stuff.

But even without doing speedruns, I think the game offers enough content to be worth the money, unless you basically spoiler yourself with guides before you even start (at which point it's getting a bit boring and mechanical, as the normal playthrough isn't that dificult once you understand most mechanics).
A big fun aspect of the game is losing horribly a lot and then learning more and more how stuff works and then at some point you just easily beat it using all your hard gained knowledge and it feels really good. But if you just look up everything, that sense of achievement will never happen and the game will probably feel a bit bland.

Two last negative points I want to mention, one is a bug the other a framerate problem. There is still a bug that can break the game a little. Like it can happen that you win, but you don't get the victory and all your dudes stop working. If you don't know that this is a bug it can get quite frustrating. The first time I actually beat the game this happened and I didn't realize it was not supposed to happen, so I spent another 20 days trying to figure out how to win until someone in the forums exaplined to me that this is a bug. (If that happens to you, just exit and start again, and it should put you before the bug happens and you should be fine from there on).
The framerate issues "luckily" only happen later on (say day 60 and upwards and usually only during blood moon nights where a lot of monsters appear), so if there wasn't an achievement for surviving 100 days most people would probably never experience it. But there is. And they do. Regardless of how good your computer rig is it seems.

I want to end with saying I had a quite magical time with this game. I bought it right when it came out and a lot of people were streaming it at that point. Since there weren't any guides available at this time it created a very unqie atmosphere, where I would hop from stream to stream watching a bit, seeing what others might have figured out that I haven't, sharing some small tips here and there myself. It really reminded me of the earlier days of gaming, when you couldn't just look up everything online but went to friends places shared and small discoveries with each others. That's something I haven't experienced in over a decade and I probably won't in quite a while. So I just want to end by shouting a big "thank you" to the devs for creating this marvelous experience with their game and I stay curious to see where they take it from here.

TL;DR : If you enjoy being a scientist, testing stuff, doing things to see what happens, learn from that, be willing to accept to fail a few times until you get it right, enjoy atmospheric pixel art and great soundtrack the this game might really be for you.
If you want to expand and grow an empire and survive a long time, don't enjoy to figure stuff and gameplay mechanics out for yourself, then you might give this game a pass (at least for now). There is more content coming, so maybe come back in 6 months and see how the game has developed by reading the latest news and content updates and see what people have to say then.

Anyway, hope this review helped give a good voerview about the good and bad aspects of the game. Please thumbs up if you find it helpful as well, so others can benefit from the reivew too :)

I don't often play this game, but when I do, it's when I'm feeling truly miserable, when the dark thoughts creep to the edge of my mind and everything becomes hopeless. It is incredible to find such simple joy in sadness, in the impermanence of Civilisation, in the meaninglessness of it all, as I wander across the empty fields I cleared of trees, piles of ancient stones covering the clear horizon atop empty green moorlands, and as the mists begin to roll in... there's just such a simple joy in all of it, away from the injustices of the world, away from your failings and missed potential. It's easy to get lost, to want to just spend the rest of your life playing such games, experiencing nothing but escapism, but one day the rent will be due, one day your friends will miss you, one day you will die... Take joy in these things, in these beautiful experiences, but don't do so at the cost of the rest of your life. When you're done, go outside, read a book, learn to draw... don't abandon the experiences that help you get through the day, but don't let them consume you. Use them to fuel you. Because even if it's all meaningless in the end, even if our lives are brief and impermanent... That does not mean there is no joy in the world. Laughter is real. Love is real. Art is real. If this is your only life, enjoy the experiences it grants you while you still can, and do what you can to make sure others can do the same without hurting them, or yourself. Kingdom is a work of art, that through its sadness, helps me to cope with my problems, and feel a little bit more joy in the world. Thank you for reading my review. I know it says 10 hours on record, but I swears it on the precious that this isn't the first time I've had this game, I just haven't always had it on this account. I swears it. Pinky promise.

Kingdom is a great game, and a very challenging one at that. Infact, one of my favourite moments is when you finally get past that day 20 blood moon for the first time. It is great value for money and my hours in game isnt a fair representation of the time i have on this game because i play it on other accounts too. 

It has a very small tutorial and then lets you explore the world however you want, so much freedom and choice! The game will punish you for even the smallest mistakes and you will quickly learn, i reset countless times on the first day of playing.

Pros:

Amazing sound

Beautiful visual design, I love how well 2D looks in this game

Days and Nights are just long enough to get what you set out to do done :)

Each day has a new challenge, literally...

Your asthmatic horse adds a real challenge

The steam achievements are really something to aim for and you will find it hard getting them all

Cons:

Very laggy at end game gameplay (due to so many archers probably)

(Some people may question this) - There is a lot of freedom ingame as the tutorial doesn't hold you back but some people argue that only being able to place towers in specific points is lack of freedom? Well i agree to a certain extent (thats why it is a con) but that is a challenge in the game! The first 2 towers are always near your castle and the others have to be planned ahead of time, you cant decide to build a wall 200 yards out the night before a blood moon! You have to THINK AHEAD.

The AI is poor. You can literally run rings around those massive ogre things and they can't hit you and just wait until daylight. Your archers venture so freaking far out at day that they don't even make it back in time at night... I'm not sure why but that needs a fix. It is frustrating.

Lack of late game challenges. I am at the point, well i was long ago, where i could win the game in the click of a button but i want to see how far my castle gets me. I could easily send my knights out to the portals and win but i want to see what the game has instore very late. At night 30+ you have probably learned how to manage your money and will be constantly overflowed in cash. This is a problem as i really can't lose past day 30, it is too easy for late game. (Maybe the monsters could be stronger and have more hp late game? instead of just trying too flood my walls and my catapult can 1-shot them all?) that is just a suggestion.

The game will crash a lot! Especially when you have lots of archers, so save every day because it has happened, when you crash and load back 8 nights ago!

Why did i buy the game?

We have all been there, watching your favourite youtuber play a brand new series and get destroyed on the first episode. Then we all think, "Ha! I could do better than that!" Well I couldn't. This game is very hard early game and as i have said, you get punished very easily. -_-

However, that wasn't the only reason, i absolutely love games where you can build massive armies and feel "powerfull". I certainly do now! If you like construction games or strategy or something like this in any way, give Kingdom a chance. It is very cheap and offers so much as each reset is randomly generated (sort of).

How to win (no spoilers)

As i have mentioned there is no tutorial but that doesn't mean go and search "how to beat kingdom" on google or youtube. The fun in this game is the fact that YOU make the mistakes and you have too complete it on your own! 

If i would recommend any strategy it would be, you can never have enough archers, don't upgrade the bridges (you will find them on your own) until you have walls passed them, find the stone wall upgrade fast (not telling you where it is ;p).

Oh ye, and don't expand too fast, i really mean it. If you expand the monsters will tear through your level 1 walls and rampage through your town. Plan your expansions, the night after blood moons is a great time to expand!

Repetition

This game is one of those that is more addicting than Candy Crush, more fun than COD or CS:GO and will keep you playing until long after midnight. It is the constant "oh i will just play one more (ingame) night because if i go to sleep now i will forget what my plan was" what you don't realise is that you say that to yourself, every, freaking, time.

you will also get times when you restart of your own decision, not the fact that monsters just took your crown, this can be many reasons but the one that first got me was when; you buy the merchant on night 2 and he gives you four builders, then you find him again very soon, and he gives you four more builders. I just restarted after that.

There will also be times when you recover from disaster, one well placed boulder from the ogres lands right ontop of you mass gathering of stupid archers but somehow he doesn't break through your last wall and dies, then you panick and spend all your money repairing.

There will be times when you recover from disaster then make the biggest mistake and have to restart anyway.

In conclusion i absolutely love this game. It is well worth the price tag, and as i said at the start i have at least 50+ hours on other accounts. I would recommend this game to anyone! Even if you have a laptop worth £10 (well a bit more) you can run this game no problem.

Thanks for reading.

I love this game.

Lately my life has been so busy, even when I have the time to sit down down and enjoy playing a game I rarely feel like doing it for more than 45 minutes or an hour. Kingdom has taken me back to what gaming use to be like for me: Losing hours of my life in a different world; Becoming completely immersed and forgetting about everything else.

It's hard for me to say exactly why this game is so great. At first it seems really basic, the entire game can be played with three buttons on the keyboard. Don't be fooled though, there is a lot of strategy here and the game will definitely kick your butt once or twice before you start getting the hang of it.

What makes this game special is not just gameplay though, it's the entire feel and atmosphere of the game. Whether or not you like pixel art, it's hard to call this game anything other than beautiful. The way day and night cycles, the sunsets, moonlight, fog, rain, clouds. Every day and night feels slightly different and it always feels special. This is complimented by the subtle yet suberb sound and music.

If you like the look of this game and think you'll enjoy it you probably will. Don't spend too much time researching it and potentially spoiling things for yourself, just know that it's a great experience and it is worth your time and money.

First off, great soundtrack. This game infuriated me for a good while due to it being unforgiving. Once a building is up, it's up even if it cuts off half your farmland. Yet, I endured and by the end of my last 37 day game, I was drowning in gold making me think that I should have walked away and just let the game play till day 100.

The secret is to build walls beyond the farm lands and campsites. As you go back and forth between both ends of your Kingdom you'll be able to continually recruit vagrants and collect gold. I had probably 20 villagers in reserve due to recruiting them each time I passed by.

Growth depends on the number of people you have to generate income, so continually recruiting new villagers is essential. Avoid expanding over the campsites by sparing each tree closests to them on both sides. Explore beyond them to the next open area and you'll likely be able to find a place to build a wall or a tree to cut down.

Can't wait to start the sequel.

[h1]This game is simple, but addicting. I wasn't sure it will last me for more than few hours, and I usually don't approach games thinking that I'll stay up all night playing, but I got lucky here. This game is all about management and choices. It'll start innocent, but quickly becomes pure evil the more you hold on.[/h1]

[b]Gameplay[/b]
You control most of the things indirectly. You'll start small, and you'll make a lot of mistakes while trying to get bigger. I can't promise you that you'll get hooked the same way I did, but after having few tries on my own, I've started seeing the game differently. It is based around trying it over and over, and I didn't get sick of it. Despite what I've heard, every part, even the beginning, becomes an endurance run. Since you have to control everything, you can't stop.

I've played it at least 15 times and every time I've just tried better. This game isn't mainly about discovering new things, but about mastering the logic it's based on. Sure, sometimes I damn the developers to hell, but I think the fundamental gameplay is good for what it is. 

[b]Controversy[/b]
There are some people that are divided about some choices, or more precisely, the lack of them. They have usually played the game for few hours and then stopped, complaining about basics, like AI, or inability to control some things. While they raise some good points, I don't think they apply here. Because the game is so simple, it is essentially based around what they don't like. And that's fine. I think what they're asking for is a more complex game overall, because this is like asking for having advanced control over Lemmings. Also, I would love more complex version of Kingdom, so I'm hoping for sequel or expansion already.

Perhaps it could include an easy mode with some additional choices, because the way I look at it, this game is supposed to be beaten by trying over and over. I can't tell if it'll last 30 hours, but there are many people that have been mesmerized by games like Binding of Isaac, which is also based around playing it over and over. I've found out the hard way, that you can overcome the odds, if you just get prepared. The more you play, the more you plan ahead - that is the way I more forward here.

Don't get me wrong. The game is difficult. But it's difficulty doesn't come from poor design decisions or blatantly unbalanced gameplay. People that drop the towel early might not be into this, but if you just hold on, and give it few more tries, where you learn how to be more efficient, you'll be rewarded with progress. When something limits you, it's made so you can work with it - just like in chess, the more planning you do, the easier your progress will be. And yes, sometimes the random generators can screw you over.

And to be honest, there are problems with the late game, where you're mainly forced to run from one corner of the map to another. Apparently, the longer you wait with destroying the portals (your main objective, after you're comfortable with your defences), the more difficult it becomes to take them down, as you're limited with numbers of your attack party, but enemy defence spawn is infinite and increases over time. This is still being discovered by many invididuals on forums, but so far it seems like you can't take your time, which adds another layer of difficulty. You have to be efficient, and really fast. Once you get past day 30, portals become almost impossible to take down - it's doable, but frustrating and time consuming, not to mention that nothing significant happens at that point and you can play for hours, just running back and forth, without any tactics you had to employ at the beginning of game. I don't recommend trying to complete the game this way.

[b]Presentation[/b]
It's pretty damn good. That is something we all agree with. Music is captivating and what more, along with the graphics it creates a great atmosphere, which I rarely see, especially in such simple game. Overall, great presentation helps you push forward as well.

[b]Verdict[/b]
This is not a mobile game. It is a PC game, and games like this are rare. The simplicity mixed with indirect influence over your growing settlement is challenging and addicting. I don't mind losing, and I don't mind trying again, until I either succeed or eventually, leave with bruises and broken bones. Either way, I see myself spending way more than 10 hours that I've spend already and every hour was filled with intense planning and resource management.

It really pains me to give this game a negative review. This game is so beautiful, it has an original central mechanic and it's so full of promise. But, as it is, it's just a frustrating mess to actually play- which was the chief problem of the original free online version, as well. The friendly AI is not quite as stone stupid as in the original, but with the more complicated mechanics of the new version the outcome is about the same- your greatest enemy in this game is your allies.

For example, there are now catapults in the game, operated by the new builders. Catapults are very strong weapons, but they attack slowly and need a builder to reset them in-between attacks. Once a catapult is constructed, your builders will move it to your outermost walls, and move it again further out if new outermost walls are erected. So, hey, let's say you have a strong inner citadel with palisades on the outskirts. Guess where your builders will put your catapults? Where they are most vulnerable! What if your outermost walls are destroyed? No, the builders will not then move the catapult back inside the walls, it's just stuck out there in the open forever. There is no way you can control any of this. Guess you have to give up layered defenses if you want to use catapults!

So, you give up having perimeter palisades so you can have your catapult behind your strong inner wall, and the horde is coming. Does the catapult wait until the mass of demons is in range for a strong crowd control shot? Nope! It fires the moment the first little lead peon touches its range, and almost always then misses hitting anything at all as its shot drops behind the front runner and ahead of the main assault. Well, that's okay really, the catapult can just fire again, right? Ah, but it's not so easy, now you have to wait for the catapult to be reset. And funny thing, while your archers are now finally smart enough to stand by your walls at night in order to defend them, your builders... not so much. So, seeing as they wander aimlessly even in the middle of a siege, it's anybody's guess how long it will take for a builder to reach your catapult and begin actually operating it for the rest of the battle.

On top of all this there appears to be an outright bug where your character is vulnerable to your own catapult's fire even on the way up, and standing next to the catapult when it fires can cause your character to fumble their crown, flinging it forward into the mob of demons on the other side of the fully-intact wall, instantly costing you the game. This has happened to me more than once.

These catapult issues are not at all isolated, but if I try and list every stupid thing the friendly AI does then this review will become a very boring novel. The friendly AI is simply totally incompetent. Furthermore, the several entirely new mechanics added to the game have no explanation associated with them at all, despite the game having a simple, straightforward, and enjoyable tutorial for the central mechanic, taken from the original game. The new mechanics are simply unexplained, and some of them are apparently vital. There are cryptic features I am still utterly stumped by, like the shield on the menu, the banner in your camp, or the statue in the forest. These aspects of the game do not feel so much poorly designed as simply unfinished, as if it was shipped in a rush before there was time to put instructions on how to play into the game.

In summation, at this time this new version of Kingdom remains, as it was before, a beautiful, creative, unique, incredibly mind-numbingly frustrating game in which you want to bang your head against the screen displaying all the pretty pretty pictures because your little men have no common sense. It is definitely fixable with some work, if the developer chooses to fix it. Here's hoping they do.

For new players, you might as well start out with Kingdom Classic, before buying Kingdom Newlands. This is a great game that only gets expanded by K:NL after a few hours of gameplay. For me, I am pretty bored with the game after a couple hours, anyway.

I really like the gameplay in Kingdom, because I am a fan of dark fantasy themes and base-building gameplay. I really like the side-view POV, too.

I think most people already own this game, since it is inexpensive and been on Steam for a long while, but anyone checking it out for the first time should add it to their library. Easy to have many hours of fun, at a very low price. However, there is no tutorial, and there are many non-obvious things about the game, so you will need to research a tiny bit in the Steam Community Area.

I enjoyed Kingdom Classic on an ubuntu linux 18.10 system, with radeon mesa graphic drivers. The game uses the Unity Game Engine, and it takes 300 MBs of diskspace. It worked well with my xbox-type gamepad controller. I encountered no technical issues while playing.

I struggled to understand how to play so I eventually looked up cheats online. It does a terrible job of explaining how to play however it is a fantastic game. Here are some things I struggled to figure out which might help you.

[spoiler][list]
[*]Skip the beginning tutorial by holding down down arrow / s
[*]You can build out of stone by finding a wooden hut and giving it gold. You may have to travel past a portal.
[*]The black horse can sprint for longer, it's not just a cosmetic change
[*]Your builders are not the brightest. If you tell them to build out of your camp at night they will and probably get caught. 
[*]You can give your knights lots of gold to keep for when they battle the portal
[*]The statues / monuments will strengthen your archers or walls respectively. The higher tiers make it last longer. They are not permanent and will need to be refreshed.
[*]Upgrading a farm will make all the farmers stay there at night. Make sure to upgrade a farm only when it is in your walls
[*]A camp will disappear if either of the two trees beside it are missing
[*]Grass spawns rabbits. Walls stop grass from spreading so make sure you build your walls and farms after it has spread.
[*]The night after a red moon there are no monsters
[*]You can build a portal for you to use after you have destroyed a monster portal. You have to try and place it where you can't build anything. After you have teleported back to camp you must give it gold quickly before it disappears.
[/list]  [/spoiler]

Hope that was helpful

In my ongoing and likely futile effort to write a Steam review for every game in my library (#18 out of 500+)... it's time for Kingdom.

Kingdom, like most really good games, is deceptively simple.

You control a king (or queen) astride a horse, and possess two abilities: you can move freely... and you can throw money at things. Your role is to scout out villagers for your new kingdom (throwing money at them), assign them to specific jobs (throwing money at the requisite toolmakers), and construct defenses (throwing money at specific landmarks). Every night, come sunset, your kingdom is beset by a horde of demons. Or monsters. But unlike the evil foes in most games, even those that purport to be all about storytelling, Kingdom's rampaging inhuman beasts actually have a *reason* to rampage--they want your stuff. The goal of the game is to spend as many of the daylit hours as you can shoring up your castle's defenses, expanding territory and generating revenue as possible in order to survive the night.

So, yeah: it's a tower defense game. But with depth.

OVERVIEW

Each unit in the game is governed by simple AI. Unaffiliated villagers will gather at camps out in the wilds. Claimed villagers will move directly to your castle and will loiter about until you give them a tool and trade. Leave them be for too long, and they'll abandon you. Archers can be staffed into watch towers, but their true utility is as hunters. During the day they will venture beyond your kingdom's walls to hunt, which generates gold, and at night they retreat behind the walls to act as your garrison, raining volleys of arrows down upon your nightly assailants. Farmers till the fields, builders build things. The key to victory lies with the knights--plate-armor clad heroes, each aided by a single squire with a longbow--who are the only offensive means at your disposal. With sufficient gold and a fully-upgraded keep, you can commission up to four knights, who then move to your kingdom's outermost walls to raise a banner. Pay a little more gold at the knights' banner to finance an offensive, and he will valiantly sally forth into the woods with whatever archers are nearby to assault the bizarre portals from which the nightly terrors emerge.

The monsters have a single overriding goal: to acquire loot. Once a monster grabs a shiny coin or fancy new hammer, it promptly turns around and retreats back to the portal it came from. You face thieves, not butchers. This predictable behavior adds a new layer of tactical depth to the game, as you can use surplus gold to bribe enemy units--transforming an invading army into a rabble, or halting a counterattack when your knights demolish a stone portals.

Each new day brings attacks both more frequent and aggressive. By mid-game (once you've destroyed at least one portal), titanic demons emerge who spew out smaller friends. While the first several days can be peaceful, by the end, things are *brutal.* Difficulty is not static, but scale's with the player's progress--the better you play, the better the enemy plays. This allows the game to cater to multiple skill levels--at least until the end-game--without the need for a difficulty slider.

All your power as monarch is invested, of course, in your crown. Because power lies where men believe it lies, and have you seen a crown lately? All gold and gleaming. Of course, portal-spawn can see and appreciate the splendor of a crown as well as you or I, and find it a tempting target. Should the king chance upon an enemy, it will immediately try to bat the crown off his or her head. Once removed, you can retake the crown if you're lucky and restore your position... and if not, you've lost it for good. Without a crown cresting your brow, you're nothing. Game over.

PROBLEMS

Sometimes (albeit rarely) the AI governing a specific unit just... won't seem to work properly. A builder will stand by some scaffolding, but won't move an inch until *another* builder starts working on it. When resources are stretched and erecting a quick palisade is the only thing standing between you and the game over screen, an idle worker is the last thing you want to see. The difficulty curve is very natural, but also very steep. A few adjustments in the options menu could make the game more palatable to gamers with less time (because for most, skill is a matter of time more than effort or ability). 

There's also not a whole lot of variety. Each game plays out in "randomized" levels that are virtually indistinguishable. Your keep sits in the middle. Go far enough to either side and you'll pass by two camps and two portals and discover a steep obsidian cliff at the edge of the world. There's no real variety--you'll be seeing the same background and foreground assets in the last minute of the game as you saw in the first. It would have been nice to see some variety--different climates or seasons, something to give some variety to the visuals.

I'd also have liked to see a bit more depth to the upgrade system. There are four or five different levels for each of your main buildings (walls, towers and the central keep) which are all fairly easy to get to quickly, which means there's less to do at the keep in the late game beyond just making sure you're earning enough money to outfit enough citizens to survive the night or launch a successful offensive.

Which plays into the rather problematic issue of not being able to undo anything. Got an archer stuck up a tower that serves no tactical purpose because it used to be the outermost border of your kingdom too weeks ago? Too bad, you can't demolish anything. Stuck with 20 builders and no archers and want to re-class some citizen? Can't do it. Expand far enough that no more camps exist to generate new citizens, but not enough manpower to take out the last portal? You'll have to start over.

PRESENTATION

Good Lord, this is one hell of a gorgeous game.

If you're rolling your eyes at that, well, I understand. I do. I've seen countless people extol the beauty of retro-style sprites and pixel-art games in the past (I'm sure I will in the future, too) and I've rolled my eyes, too. Well, figuratively. Most of the time when I assess the pixel-art in these games, I find it to exist in artistry's stead, not for artistry's sake. Don't have an artist, the modus operandi seems to be, use pixel art.

But Kingdom is a rare exception. In motion, it's minimalist aesthetic is breathtaking. It is a vibrant, stunning world--almost all of it animated. No more pixels go into any object than need be. The ever-important crown atop your monarch's head? Nine pixels. The horse you ride? It's drawn at a resolution that would have seemed inexcusably low back in the Super Nintendo era. But I cannot count the number of times I heard it snort, wave its tails, start panting with exhaustion and slow to a trot, or bend over to munch on some grass where I lost sight of the literal image in front of my eyes and saw instead saw a flesh-and-blood charger, sweating in the sun. The pixel art, animation, music and sound effects all weave together to form... a dream. An unreal, tantalizing, almost hypnotic thing that comes to life as we behold it.

FINAL COMMENT

As I hope I've made clear, Kingdom is a very simple game. You play as a person on a horse who can throw money at things with the expectation that they'll behave in an expected fashion. You must use this epic superpower to build a keep, expand it into a kingdom, and fend off a daily horde or nightmarish invaders from... elsewhere. The underlying mechanics are simple and predictable and allow for a surprising amount of depth. Everything comes together very neatly into a single package that is enormously engrossing, fantastically fun, and deeply challenging. If you've read to this point already--well, first, thank you for you patience--I most likely don't need to say it, but I will anyway: Kingdom is an amazing game and is absolutely worth both your money and your time.

It's an enjoyable game with a simple but satisfying gameplay experience, beautiful pixel art, and generally fun mechanics which blend Tower Defense and Base Building. It's worth 10 dollars to kill some time and see how long you can stave off your inevitable doom. However, the game is in desperate need of a patch to fix some of its glaring problems; and believe me, it has a load of gameplay shortcomings which become painfully obvious after an hour or two. 

- The AI is abysmal. I mean painfully and blitheringly horrible. I found myself dying not because of the enemies, but because my workers would charge mindlessly into oncoming hordes of ogres to do something stupid that I didn't want them to do. I lost my best run around day 35-ish because all 6 of my workers charged into a golem as they attempted to repair a crappy tier-1 wall. Another time I died because a troll snuck around a wall somehow and the AI was too stupid to turn around to shoot it, so it walked almost completely unopposed into my base and wrecked everything.

- Further, you have no control over anything your units do, or even over the type of units they become. All of your archers dead? Sucks to be you, the game thinks you want farmers. Don't want your workers charging into an enemy horde to load a catapault or fix a wall? Meh, oh well. Don't want your farmers wondering into the wilderness to farm and then getting picked off like sleeping hens when the enemy shows up? Nope, can't stop that.

- The above two issues wouldn't even be issues if there was a way to grow your population on your own, but you can't do that. To get villagers you have to find camps and pay the campers to come live in your village. The problem with this system is that villagers are an extremely finite rescource and, as I said above, they kill themselves like lemmings and there is nothing you can do to stop this. 

It's a fun game, it really is, but it feels like a mobile game in that it is hampered by bizzare shortcomings which cripple the gameplay once your past day 20-ish. If a fan would make a mod, or the dev would make a patch, this game could be amazing. As it is though, you may find it to be worth the 10 dollar price tag, but I can't really recommend the game in its current state.

Kingdom is not a bad game, for what it's worth. The mechanics are surprisingly fun, the concept is great, the art design is good and it's unique; there are few, if any, games like Kingdom. However, despite those things, I did not enjoy this game.

I have two main reasons for this: the game is overtuned in terms of difficulty and it jumps you. Kingdom is basically a game of setting up AI for success, and given that the AI is kind of dumb (as in, doesn't always run back to camp when monsters are coming-kind of dumb) the way to do this is overwhelming odds. That means making archers. A lot of archers. It also means that you need to be careful with expanding. Which is fine once you figure that out (it will probably lead to your first loss, given that the game tells you nothing and you might not know what you need to do).

However, here's what happened to me. I did all this, and I did pretty great. Had plenty of stuff at my borders, had destroyed my first portal and made my first teleporter. So I went on to the second portal, on the other side: it was a bit far away, but I could make it. So I sent a party out to destroy the portal, like I did the first. They destroyed it, it was fine, but after I did so, suddenly I couldn't go into the forest anymore without a huge wave off things coming after me. Clincher is, you have to go into the forest to recruit more people (as well as create a teleporter out of the destroyed portal).

A couple of nights later, I was dead. A wave too big for my defenses, which I hadn't been able to rebuild, overwhelmed me.

Thing is, even before losing, I was already fighting the game's systems. Getting recruits home when they slowly walk towards your home base, not being able to get builders to return home until it's too late, having to go around collecting coins all the time in order to do things and most importantly, having to recruit so many people just because you need those overwhelming numbers on your side. So when you go through these hassles (that are just flaws of the game), and then it surprises you with a huge challenge that comes out of nowhere? It made me demotivated. To play it all from the start again just for something new to catch me unawares is simply not appealing gameplay to me.

Maybe the game would've been more rewarding if I stuck it out. Maybe if I would've been more resilient, I could've liked Kingdom in the end. But at the same time, the game did fail to keep me interested. If the game would've had a more gradual challenge, I would've probably been on board. As it is, simply put, this game is frustrating for the wrong reasons. Hopefully they did something to adress this in the sequel.

[b]This game has some of the most emotionally-engaging, postcard-esque ambient environments that I have ever witnessed.[/b] The music is [i]literally[/i] a perfect match with the absolutely gorgeous pixel art work. [i]When I load it up, it transports me to the fairytale.[/i] Few games do that. The attention is in the details, too. The way things move, and shifts from night to day. I cannot stop looking at it. It has a very zen way about it.

The [i]experience[/i] alone is worth the ten bucks. Especially with headphones.

---

Now, lets get into the review about the game, and to some of the debatably negative points.

At the outset, this game [i]screams[/i] mobile to me, because of the minimal controls. Minimal controls typically limit the amount of complexity you can have (and yeah, there are outliers, but in general thats the case). I argued ad nauseam with the devs about the mobile issue, which can be found on the forums. 

The minimalism isn't just in the controls, though. It is also with the interface. The game [i]literally[/i] tells you nothing onscreen as far as your clan status (no number of recruits, or a breakdown of any kind - it doesn't even give you a gold count per se).

There is a fine line in roguelite games in regards to hand-holding. If you offer too much, there is little reward for self-discovery that so many of us roguelite/like fans crave. If you offer too little, confusion takes over and we all begin to really question how smart the game is. "Are there deeper mechanics here, or is it oversimplified?" (ie. Do archers in towers [i]actually[/i] have better accuracy? I have no idea. This goes on and on.

[i]The bottom line here: I wish you had more control over the game. It would violate the idea of minimalism, but would be a tradeoff for higher complexity, and thus strategy.[/i]

Another major gripe is the AI. This is true. I have no idea how to fix this, other than better coding. To me, this translates to having much more fun in the early game, than in the mid- to late-game, where it becomes so much more important to not have hoardes of your troops doing stupid things. 

This brings me to my final point: the game might benefit from time speeding up the longer you play, or something. Its a slow grind. Kind of like when you die after surviving a million days in [i]Don't Starve[/i], its really hard to start fresh and be excited about it.

Some overall suggestions that I have heard, that I think are real possibilities:
[i]1. You should be able to hunt, to help kill time, and increase interactivity.
2. There should be meta-game unlocks. Could be everything from cosmetic clothing to better gear and buildings.
3. It might be worth considering just having the horse be able to run forever.
4. Implement a 'peaceful' or 'easy' game mode.[/i]

[b]Overall, this game has balance issues - but wow they really did pull off a beautiful project that hopefully could slide into something truly great.[/b] I doubt the developers will change things significantly (what we have now is probably what we will have forever, more-or-less), but oh boy is the potential there.

[b]I totally recommend it for the experience alone.[/b]

It's a resource management game, but with only one resource. Gold! 
Only 3 buttons to play. Very easy to control, but quite hard to manage.

You start, and barely get any explanation, just the very basics. This pretty much leaves a lot up to trial and error. It is part of the fun though! So, as you ride through the forest with nothing else than your trusted horse, golden crown and waving cape, you soon find 10 gleaming coins, which you pick up as you pass them. With those coins you can upgrade your campfire and recruit the 2 beggars next to it, by tossing them a coin as the noble king that you are. When your fire is upgraded, you can outfit your citizens with a hammer or a bow, which turns them into workers or bowmen. As you keep upgrading, more tools become available. 

When you start exploring the woods, you will find more beggars to recruit. Some rabbits to hunt for your bowmen to yield money. Recruit loyal people. Equip them wisely. Expand thy borders. Defend with care! And drive the trolls back.

I feel conflicted about this game. It's great to look at and easy to learn, but its also very difficult to actually win and usually leaves you watching helplessly as your kingdom falls down all around you. I still enjoy playing it, but I do so somewhat grudgingly. 
On the one hand, as many others have noted, the game's first impression is very good. The atmosphere it creates for you as you first jump into its world, from the supurb music to its wonderfully done 2D graphical style, is excellent. It's unique, and very immersive. You really do get the feeling of building a settlement from scratch in a mysterious and dangerous fantasy world, etching your kingdom and its people to victory.
As you start playing for a while though, Kingdom's problems become increasingly apparent. And they are not small problems. As a result of some seriously flawed design decisions, you come to realize that the game does almost everything it can to make you fail in incredibly irritating ways. It lets you hire citizens, but not control them, meaning they'll make incredibly stupid decisions like abandoning their posts at the worst possible times or let themselves die helplessly outside your walls. It lets you move around on your horse, but makes the world so big that it takes a huge portion of your day just to get from one spot to another on the map, all while your horse is constantly slowing down because it's too tired. It lets you send out raiding parties, but they too will walk so painfully slow that it will usually take an entire day or more for them to get to their destination. This means that unless you set them loose immediately after a Blood Moon, they will all die in transit, and you will then inevitably lose. 
In general, this is a game that can only be beaten if you know how to exploit all of its inadvertant weaknesses, and do everything perfectly the same way every time. Its simplicity, charming at first. works against it in the end.

I was initially lured in by the game's cute premise and aesthetic, but unfortunately, its bag of tricks was exhausted rapidly, and after unlocking the limited amount of content available, the late-game turned out to be highly tedious. Once your kingdom stretches across the map, it takes very long to get anything done. Your units need an entire in-game day to get to near the edge of the map from your base in the middle - which might not be a problem in itself, if their AI weren't so dumb.

Your builders, for instance, have no survival instinct whatsoever and will march blindly into death's maw so long as there's a construction job queued up on the other side of it, so once you have a big kingdom, you'll assuredly lose those builders if you don't queue up the job at just the right time of day. Once they're gone, a new set of builders will notice there's an unclaimed build job available and head in to get mowed down, until you have no more builders left.

In a similar vein, if you upgrade a farm to a farmhouse, your farmers will congregate there at night regardless of whether it's actually safe to do so or not, instead of seeking shelter at your main base, and will consequently get slaughtered there every night if you don't have defenses built. The game does not feature the ability to cancel build jobs or demolish or deactivate buildings, and the issues are further compounded since manpower is a scarce, slowly-renewable resource in the game.

The poor AI is not the only issue that can lead to frustration in the late-game. As you expand your kingdom, the wilderness camps that function as your source of manpower in the game disappear, leaving you less able to recover from setbacks and potentially leading to a slow, yet inevitable and tedious loss by attrition. As the distances within your kingdom increase, you can end up spending a lot of time running back and forth around the map without a lot of progress to show for it. You can't send parties of more than 8 units to attack enemy portals - it seems peculiar that the strength of the enemy defenses scales up over time, but the amount of troops you can use when launching an attack is fixed at such a low amount.

Ultimately, [b]Kingdom[/b] possesses an interesting initial premise and a charming aesthetic, and could become a good game if more content is added and its more egregious issues get fixed, but I find it hard to recommend it in its current state.

Fantastic, lovely, scary, calm. This game manages to project calm, beatiful melancholy and contemplative planning while almost simultaneously giving off a sense of rush as you explore, maintain, expand and oversee your titular Kingdom.

Replayability is there to be found: randomized setting for each game requires some variance to your broader strategy and priorities. The gently challenging nature of the game ensures all Kingdoms must come to an end, and even after a long game of struggle and survival it feels like there is still something I could do better on a fresh start. Meanwhile the achievements hint there are still things that can be accomplished in the first ~20 minutes of the game that I did not accomplish during my massive Kingdom that lasted two hours the previous night.

Clear design with minimalist controls (left, right to walk - double tap and hold to run; down (tap or hold) = action), beautiful scenery and effects pegged as "modern pixel art" by the dev and the light soundtrack well-suited for the overall feel of the game all add up to a gripping experience.

First off, let me begin be stating that this game in its current state is a great indie game, I've had loads of fun with it so far. It's definitely a unique concept put forth. However, I would not recommend buying it, at the moment. It's late game is, fairly broken, this is attirbuted to a few things:

1) Lack of unit control. Now, I understand that the aim of the game is to have only 3 keys to play, a simplistic approach. And I applaud that approach because even with very few controls, there are many concepts that can be learned and played from within the game. But as the game progresses, and the enemies get much harder, you find that not being able to control where units guard or attack is an EXTREME frustation. One example are towers, a good concept, but without being able to control the units within them, they become a waste of effort and time, which leads me to my second point.

2) Building management. To put it shortly, there is none. You build them by using your gold, and that's is it. As far as destroying them for a refund, or controlling what units occupy them, be it farmers or archers, they go in and out as they please, which is TERRIBLE late game. The concept of towers in this game is broken because of that fact, I have dozens of archers sitting way behind the front lines doing zip for the entire game, precious archers which could be much needed in portal raids. In its current state, it is more benefical to completely ignore tower mounds and not build them, as it wastes archers AND leaves them vulnerable to flying enemies.

3) Difficulty. While I admire a good challenge, the difficulty spike in this game is just plain ludicrous. The waves get extremely difficulty around day 30, and if the game goes on for too long, it becomes a literal stalemate with victory being a certain impossibility.

4) Lack of force replenishment. The only way to recruit new subjects in this game is through forest camps. However, at a certain point in the game, forest camps completely disappear! Which basically means you need to win with your current force count, which is quite literally impossible. Most games there will be at least one camp left late game, but even then your forces are destroyed at a higher rate for you ever to go back to positive gain at that late in the game. There needs to be a mechanic for you to recruit forces within your walls.

As it currently stands, it feels as if the devs didn't put much time into testing each mechanic, because if they had they most certainly wouldn't have kept it the way it is. I don't mind the difficulty level of the game when it starts to progress, but certain things are just annoying and unfair to deal with. If most of my biggest grievances are handled with in the upcoming dlc, I will be a happy camper and happily take this review down. Until then, I think it is extremely important to rebalance the entire game.

"Kingdom" is a town defense survival game where you take the role of a King or Queen who must build a kingdom all the same while protecting it from evil demonic forces. It's similar to "Craft The World", but you do not have nowhere nearly as much as freedom - which is what ultimately holds the game down for me.

Pros:
+ Excellent soundtrack
+ Beautiful visual design: It's one of the best 2D graphics I've seen in a game, starting from the sky design to the reflection of the landscape on the river on the bottom of the screen. It's something to behold.
+ Fantastic, yet challenging first few hours of gameplay

Cons:
- No freedom: Walls and Towers used to defend your town may only be built in specific areas, so you cannot build them wherever you want
- Maps are procedurally generated; it sometimes places the foundations for walls and towers in really terrible positions. The most efficient way to defend your city is to place a Tower behind a Wall so that while the enemies try to break your wall, your archers can take down the enemies. But sometimes, there might not be any tower foundation behind a wall foundation, which makes you really question such bizarre design decisions.
- Absolutely worthless AI: The AI is designed to get behind your walls as soon as night falls. However, sometimes your archers simply wander off into the forest and gets eliminated by the enemy units. It's really frustrating.
- Lack of Depth: Once you have figured out how to manage your gold and workers, the game stops progressing. You realize that there is nothing left to discover.
- Empty Spaces in your Kingdom: Once you start expanding your Kingdom, you realize that much of it is filled by empty spaces. Buildings can only be built on specific areas as mentioned above, and sometimes you will have this vast open area without any foundation at all, leaving it completely empty. It is a chore to ride through those empty areas.
- Tedious and Time-Consuming: You cannot build forward outposts. If a citizen loses their tool after being attacked by an enemy (e.g. Bow, Hammer), they have to walk ALL THE WAY back to town, which is like a thousand miles away, and get their tools from there. Your character must be present wherever you want to spend gold; which means if you notice that you have to go somewhere to recruit settlers, but some settlers in your town needs weapons, you have to do either one. You can't prepare items for settlers while exploring.

These are just a few bizarre design decisions I personally couldn't wrap my head around. I could probably name 10 more (e.g. Ogre enemies causing your clumped up archers which you have no control over to lose all their weapons at once, and if there are two ogre enemies, you can lose over 10 archers at once). The worst of all is that the game will stop progressing for you, and every single in-game day starts to feel the same as the other. It becomes a chore.

Until there are some major renovations, avoid this game if you're looking for something with more freedom.

Kingdom is one of those games that remind a player as to why indie games are so special. They might not have the biggest budget, nor may they even follow what most people demand in this day ion age. However, indie games have the ability to surprise you, and prove its innovations through creative minds. Kingdom helps be a friendly reminder to that, for it is definitely one of the most treasured games in my library now. 

     First off: I want to say that this game is not for everyone. It is a serious trial and error game, and will leave you feeling crushed and defeated multiple times. Unlike games that build as time goes on, this one will restart from the very beginning once you have a game over. Not only that, but it can be very hard to find a system that works at first, especially when it is so easy to feel lost at times. Much like an arcade game: you have one shot at victory, or you lose it all. 

      However, this game truly feels rewarding the closer you get to reaching your goals. A mix of strategy and exploration, this game builds the longer your kingdom survives. Just as you have thought that you have discovered everything, there is something right around the corner that you have missed. Top that off with some gorgeous pixel art and calming music, and you have yourself a game that is worthy of your time and patience. 

      Kingdom: Classic Edition may not be a triple A game, nor a masterpiece. However, it may help bring old gamers back to a simpler time. A time where there were no long tutorials and save files, and a time where the best way to master the game was to try-try again. A time where you do not worry about starting a new game, and only focus on beating the game. Even if I have beaten the game, I will gladly revisit this game to rekindle that nostalgic feeling. Until then, I hope that this review helps to encourage those to experience this game for themselves.

The way this game works is very basic. You're a king or queen founding a kingdom. You use coins to recruit people to your kingdom, build structures and defenses and train your people, and you get coins through hunting, farming, and chests you sometimes get. There are 4 portals, 2 on each side of your settlement, that spawn enemies at night that attack your camp, and your archers and walls must hold them off. The goal is to grow your kingdom and eventually destroy the portals.

When I first got this, I played it for a while and couldn't stop throughout my whole first run. I lasted 20-something days, and even though I knew I should be going to bed, it kept me playing. It was a lot of fun! But eventually, I grew my kingdom too large too fast, I tried to destroy some portals too early and my kingdom was destroyed. OK, I thought. It's my first run. I'll do better next time.

And I did. But that's where the game lost me. Because after the basics, the game doesn't get any more complex. You build some walls, train some archers, rince, repeat. You do some other stuff too, but it's all the same thing, really. And all that would be OK and I would play through the game a couple of times and be satisfied since it's so cheap, but you get into the issue of awful controls. Well, I can't say "awful." Let's just say, "nonexistent."

You can do 2, maybe 3 things with your character. Move left or right (and sprint/gallop) and drop coins. Where you drop the coins is how you build: place them at your campfire to upgrade your main building, the boyer to make more bows for archers, etc. But that's it. All your subjects act according to their own crappy AI. You can't direct your archers to one side or the other, so if there's a huge attack from one side and nothing on the other? Don't worry, your flank will be safe because you have a big group of archers watching that side while the other is overrun. Did you have a builder out chopping down trees or building something outside the wall? Half the time he'll just stand there until night and get attacked by monsters (losing his hammer that you had to pay to build, and then the coin you paid him to join you, causing him to wander off into the night, not your subject anymore). Did you build a watchtower at what was once the edge of your kingdom, only to expand, ;eaving the watchtower standing pointlessly in the middle of your kingdom? Well, you just lost an archer forever, because if they climb into a tower, they never come down, and you can't destroy the tower.

This lack of being able to micromanage things is completely riduclous and totally ruins an otherwise fun game. I don't understand the developer's motivation to not include some sort of move command for individual villagers. Even at times when the AI isn't shoddy, it's so easy to send a worker outside your kingdom for something and then have it take too long and have them caught out at night. But can you have them just come back to the safety of the walls early? Nope! Too bad. They'll stand and watch as they're attacked by monsters. The description says it's a "strategy/resource management" game, but there's so little you're able to do in terms of strategy I feel they should just leave that part out.

I really wanted to like this, because it looks beautiful and the gameplay is fun, but the lack of any sort of control whatsoever over your people is completely unacceptable.

I've done three unsuccessful runs through this game so far. I believe that to be one of the draws of this game, as each playthrough is difficult but educational, as each time I make different mistakes trying to expand and build at that perfect pace. It reminds me of games like [i]FTL[/i] and [i]This War of Mine[/i]. If you enjoyed those games, I absolutely recommend this to you.

The difficulty in this game comes mainly from two points: its lack of any formal tutorial, and its lack of any control over the game.

I find it refreshing that a game, especially one this short, skips the tutorial and lets the player discover the game's intricacies for themselves. Unfortunately (or perhaps fortunately), this will generally force players to have an unsuccessful first couple of playthroughs, as they will struggle with finding out what each purchase does and the impact on the game.

The other, and more important, difficulty lies in the little control the player has over the village. Aside from building infrastructure and supplying tools, you have little to do but watch your brave men defend the village at night, or watch your incompetent men blunder through hordes of bloodthirsty monsters. While one can develop a mental checklist and strategy to prevent any mistakes, the villagers have terrible survival instincts and your success in the game does depend on them, however reckless and slow they may be.

I found it an enjoyable few hours, but the distinct lack of controls and direction (both of which I consider a redeeming feature in this game) are sure to frustrate people with very little patience. 

I give this game a solid 6/10. Very strong game, well worth the price (especially on sale). But be warned, this game requires diligence and patience to truly enjoy.

-My mangonel bugged twice, where I wasn't given the option to build another one, and my old one was just sitting there with no worker interacting with it. Kingdom Classic is a simple yet satisfying game that draws you in to push further into the game and see to its end. This is a game where you attempt to survive and figure out what you’re doing, until you inevitably fall, learn from your mistakes, and try again; things are also mixed up on the map to keep new games a little more interesting. The main selling point is its simplicity in gameplay, which may seem like a bad thing, but does it in a way that’s fun and somewhat addicting; it’s fun playing slowly the first time and observing what happens in the game. The graphics also fit the theme, with pixel graphics that look quite beautiful, and there’s attention put into the background and foreground too. The ambient music fits well with the setting and is a nice accompaniment to the gameplay.

There are some drawbacks to the lack of explanations on how things work in the game, such as if it’s not immediately obvious what something does or not even being aware of a mechanic. This may necessitate using a guide, which I hate.

If you’re looking for a simple and relaxing game to spend some time on, this game is a decent start.

Kingdom: Classic is a great little game that has you build and protect a small settlement from dark & greedy creatures.

While I certainly would suggest getting the newer version, as it has more features & changes overall, this classic is certainly worth trying, especially for being free at the time of reviewing. 

The overall gameplay loop is not that difficult nor expansive after playing for enough time, but the main gameplay and enjoyment comes from arguably trying to defend your settlement for as long as possible, while also planning ahead as to what you need to do next without over expanding and risking your citizens lives. 

You can unlock some new things overtime such as a faster/different mount, but there isn't too much in the way of global unlocks that will help you heavily, as most of the gameplay just comes down to strategy, and expanding and upgrading your settlement as much as possible before all hell breaks loose during the major "raids" every few in-game days when the blood moon rises.

In terms of music, the soundtrack is great, and has a calming charm to it which certainly fits the beautiful scenery.

The only real negative I can see is that It can be frustrating at times if you accidentally place a work order, and one of your citizens goes to do it when you don't want them to, but that's apart of some of the skill needed to know when to do things without risking a possible loss. Otherwise, there isn't too much that hurts the game.

Overall, I highly suggest trying Kingdom: Classic if you've never played it before, but I would only suggest doing so if you get it on sale, as you would be better off buying the newer one.

I feel weird about this game. I love playing it, and I love challenging and tactical games. I love city builders and the likes as well, so this is right up my alley.

First of all the gameplay's interesting  and unique, there's only one resource and 4 buttons (left, right, spend money, gallop). I recommend you don't read any guides or anything if you want to discover everything by yourself, because that is part of Kingdom's charm: It throws you into an unknown world with a bare bones tutorial and lets you figure it out by yourself. That might put some off, but I loved it. The atmosphere is incredibly immersive, it makes you just want to sit there and take it all in. But you can't, there's stuff trying to kill you.

My main issue with the game is that the later you go on into the game, the less it becomes about meaningful, tactical choices with high consequences, and the more it becomes about performing repetitive tasks to survive against impossibly huge waves. You reach the tech ceiling at about day 10, and from there it's just spamming the same units non stop. However, the devs are still working on the game, and it looks like they're plannign on making the end game more interesting.

Despite these shortcomings, the game's incredibly engaging. If anything, just for being the most minimalistic and gorgeous genuinely hard tactical game I've ever played, Kingdom is worth a look.
